title: The Gotham Dutch
description: The easiest Dutch Defense to learn, based on an early trade and a very straightforward setup of pieces. Harder to play above 2000 elo, but before that - fantastic!

lessons.title: White Plays the 2 Knights Setup (Nc3 + Nf3)

r4rk1/p1pp2p1/1pn1pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPP2/P.text:
And we won't have any problem at all in achieving the ...e5-push. 

...Re8 and ...Kh8 are some improving moves that you should consider depending on how the game progresses.

In general, you'll have better prospects because of the pawn structure.

You could even consider ...g5 at some point, but it's useful to prepare that move with ...Kh8.

r4rk1/pbpp2p1/1pn1pq1p/5p2/P1PP4/2P1PN2/.text:
We can control that square.

If 12.d5, 12...Na5 and White's central pawn play is dubious.

At any rate, even if d5 isn't played, we'll want to play something like ...Na5 and ...d6 to continue improving our position, controlling central squares, and having our knight not block the bishop.

rn2k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5P2/2PP4/2P2P2/P1.text: This helps us gain yet another positional edge.

rn2k2r/p1pp2p1/1p3q1p/5p2/2PP4/2P2P2/P1Q.text:
We can now just recapture on f5 and get ready to continue development. 

If 12.Qe2+, I like 12...Kf7, with the idea of 13...Re8. 

We'll go ...Nc6 after that, but we'll also castle kingside followed by ...Nc6 if White doesn't give the check on e2.

rn2k2r/pbpp1qp1/1p2p2p/4Pp2/2PP4/2P2N2/P.text:
The bishop can be developed to e2.

White's best idea is just to castle since they don't have any good pawn moves to make.

I suggest we castle as well.

rn2k2r/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/4Pp2/2PP4/2P2N2/P.text:
Many players like gaining space. 

But space doesn't always constitute a better position.

The queen on f7 helps control the d5-square. 

Even though it looks like it doesn't have much scope, it's deceptively active.

rn2k2r/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5P2/2PP4/2P2N2/P1.text:
Taking on f5 does also seem enticing for White, because they are splitting our pawns.

But taking on f3 is strong!

rn3rk1/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPP2/P.text: White recaptures, with a structural disadvantage now.

rn3rk1/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PPb3/2PBPN2/.text:
But here I like the strong 11...Be4, stopping White's e4 idea. 

White is advised not to take on e4 because of the x-ray on the f2-pawn. 

We'll go ...d6 and ...Nd7. When the time is right, maybe even ...e5 could be played.

Black has strong prospects and can even go for a kingside attack.

rn3rk1/pbp2qp1/1p1pp2p/4Pp2/2PP4/2P2N2/P.text:
This is why I had said that having space isn't always being 100% better. The advanced pawn can be undermined! 

We'll continue development with ...Nd7 and ...Kh8, just to be extra safe with our king in case something could get on its same diagonal. 

After exd6 cxd6, we'll also have a semi-open c-file to place a rook on with moves like ...Rac8.

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2p1qp/5P2/2PP4/2PB1N2/P.text: If White tries trading one of the pawns to get out of their troubles...

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2p2p/5P2/2PP4/2PB1N2/P1.text:
We've got another double attack. 

Black is completely winning.

The move e4 cannot be played so readily, especially with g2 hanging.

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPN2/P.text:
11.Qc2 is logical as it contributes to the e4-push.

Against it, we have ideas of ...Bxf3. 

These ideas are possible when the queen moves away from d1 at other points in this opening, not only at move 11.
11.Re1 seeks to control the center and support the e4-pawn push at some point.

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PPP3/2PB1N2/.text:
11.e4 is a mistake here, played too early.

We have a double attack using an x-ray on the e4-pawn!

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/P1PP4/2P1PN2/.text: If White attempts to get their pawn rolling and expand on the queenside...

rnb1k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PPP3/2P2N2/.text:
After White achieves their predictable e4-pawn push...

We won't capture, letting them centralize their queen. 

Rather, we'll just develop.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P1PN2/P4.text:
White could just be solid and play e3 to develop their light-squared bishop. 

We can castle here. Although White has their pawns on dark squares, our pawns are on light squares, which helps fight the influence of White's light-squared bishop. 

Once again: control of e4 is what we're aiming for here in the Dutch.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P2N2/P1Q.text:
Remember how earlier I mentioned that e4 was a pawn break that White may try going for? 

Well, putting the queen on c2 supports this idea, so you may see this being played.

Because we already have three pawns on light squares, the best square for our bishop has to be b7.

rnb1k2r/pppp2q1/4p3/5pB1/2PPn2P/2P1P3/P4.text:
But White has no compensation for the piece.

This should be an easy win.

rnb1k2r/ppppq3/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2P1P3/P4PP.text:
White continues to develop.

We unpin and attack the bishop.

rnb2rk1/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P1PN2/.text:
White castles.

We get our bishop on the long diagonal. 

It's worth noting that if you see d5 in some instances, like in this one, you can just push ...e5 and you'll have pawns that are more dangerous.

rnb2rk1/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPN2/.text:
Qc2 is an idea that certainly looks and feels natural for d4 players.

In this case, it's played around 140 times in the database, sitting at around 11%.

We'll get our bishop on the long diagonal.

Castling is now the most popular move, played around 65% of the time. 

White is just developing.

And now we can get our bishop to b7 and control the e4-square even further.

rnb2rk1/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P1PN2/P3.text:
The more modest Be2 is also possible, but this shouldn't be at all challenging. 

It doesn't fight for control of e4.

We can go for our fianchetto.

rnb2rk1/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPN2/P4.text:
In d4 openings, the d3-square is often seen as the optimal square for White's light-squared bishop. 

However, against the Dutch, this doesn't exactly work because the Dutch f-pawn blocks the diagonal.

This is the most popular move here, sitting at 62% in this position.

Once again, thanks to our Dutch pawn formation, b7 will be the best square for the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pB1p/5p2/2PP4/2P2N2/P3P.text:
The most popular move is White simply agreeing to the trade, played 50% of the time.

We're happy with our opening situation because our queen gets developed and we avoid doubling the pawns.

As a result, we have a position in which our grip of the e4-square gives us some bragging rights.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5p2/2PP3B/2P2N2/P3.text:
7.Bh4 is played 30% of the times, probably because people just don't see the danger.

We can simply win the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
The most popular move is 5.Bg5, pinning our own knight in return.

It sits at 31% in the database.

I suggest we move forward with our idea of damaging the pawns since White's Bg5 idea isn't all that effective.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2P2N2/P3P.text:
White recaptures, and we should attack the bishop here. 

The point is that after giving up our dark-squared bishop in the Dutch—seeing as our pawns are mostly on light squares—we would be happy if White gives up their dark-squared bishop as well.

rnbqk2r/pppp4/4pn1p/5pN1/2PP3B/2P5/P3PPP.text:
White could try to get two pawns for the piece and a pin on the f6-knight.

We should take the piece.

rnbqk2r/pppp4/4pn1p/6p1/2PP1p2/2P2NB1/P3.text:
And we'll go up a piece. 

We still have to consolidate because the diagonal to our king is a bit weak, but moves like ...Qe7 will help us against Qd3, Qc2 or Qb1 ideas.

rnbqk2r/pppp4/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2P5/P3PPPP/.text:
White gets their pin.

But 9...Qe7 is a great defensive resource to simply consolidate this material advantage and get rid of any counterplay.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
The two knights is now the most popular setup, being played nearly 28% of the time, which accounts for more than 1,000,000 games! 

The variation I recommend here is 4...Bb4, with the following ideas:

We increase the grip on e4 by pinning their one piece that controls it, make d5 harder to play for White, and damage White's structure.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
On the other hand, White often puts their knight on c3 (71% of the time).

Further down the line, White may have ideas of d5 or e4, and this knight helps support those pawn breaks.

3...e6 helps control the d5-square to make the move d5 not so easy for White, while possibly preparing ...d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
2.c4 is by far the most popular move. 

Many 1.d4 players are taught to move their d- and c-pawns together to control the center, just like 1.e4 players like playing e4 and d4.

Throughout this course, we will be developing our knight on the f6-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the Gotham Dutch course, get ready to face positions where you will be able to show your tactical ability with the Black pieces. 

In the Gotham Dutch, we will fianchetto our queenside bishop.

In this first study, we will go over one of the most natural and popular setups that White can play: developing both knights to c3 and f3.

lessons.title: White Plays the 2 Knights Setup With 5.Bd2

3r1rk1/p1p3pp/1p3n2/2P5/2P5/P1B1qP2/2Q1B.text:
And when White recaptures...

The threat is checkmate on f2.

3r1rk1/p1p3pp/1p6/2P5/2P3P1/P1B5/2Q1Bq1P.text:
Because there's checkmate. 

If you win a game like this, you have to leave a $10 tip when I'm live on Twitch.

3r1rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p3n2/2P5/2P2p2/P1B1PN2/.text:
If our knight is taken...

We can just take on e3. 

We're going after the king. Who cares about material!

3r1rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p3n2/2P5/2P5/P1B1PN2/2Q.text:
If White recaptures...

This check puts pressure on c3 so the queen cannot block.

3r1rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p3n2/2n2p2/1PP5/P1B1PN2.text:
It seems like 13.b4 kicks our knight out...

But we don't have to move away!

3r1rk1/pbp3pp/1p3n2/2P5/2P5/P1B1qN2/2Q1B.text:
16.Be2 is forced.

And now we can take on f3.

3r1rk1/pbpnq1pp/1p3n2/5p2/2P5/P1B1PN2/1P.text:
If the queen moves out of the discovered attack...

The queen can still come under fire!

r2q1rk1/pbpn2pp/1p1pp3/5p2/2PPn3/P1B1PN2.text:
And we should continue with our development.

Black is doing well here.

r4rk1/pbpnq1pp/1p3n2/5p2/2P5/P1B1PN2/1P3.text:
White wants to get castled.

But we won't let them get away so easily!

rn1q1rk1/pbp3pp/1p1pp3/5p2/2PP4/P1P1PN2/.text:
We play ...d6 to control the e5-square.

Our knight is coming to the a5-square via c6.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2Pn2/5p2/2P5/P1B2N2/1.text:
Taking on e6 is by far the most popular.

And we can play in gambit style!

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/2BBPN2/.text:
And now we jump into the e4-square with the healthy prospect of taking on c3 and damaging White's pawns.

If 10.Bxe4, ...fxe4 kicks the knight out of f3 and we can defend the e4-pawn after Nd2.

And if a move like 10.Rc1 is played, we can develop with ...d6 and ...Nd7.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/P1B1PN2.text:
Castling is the most popular move here, but not objectively the best because it allows you to get everything you want.

We should just double the pawns!

That's why castling isn't good.

White usually just defends with the queen.

Since the bishop is defended and we can take it on the next move, we won't spend time taking it right now. 

Instead, we'll improve our position with the moves that we know make sense in our Dutch, like ...d6 to control e5.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/P1BBPN2.text:
White castles. 

Don't worry about 10.Bxe4. If this happens, 10...fxe4 gives you an open f-file!

We can double the pawns.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2NBPN2.text:
And after White castles, I don't like the fact that if we just play ...d6 here White can go d5 in many of these positions. 

With White having pressure on f5, them playing d5 undermines the f-pawn's defender.

So I like just taking here.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B1PN2.text:
9.Be2 occurs in 54% of games.

White simply wants to castle.

We can jump into the center and attack the bishop.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1BBPN2.text:
This bishop move occurs less, around 28% of the time.

White wants to control the e4-square, but we've got the upper hand in this regard.

This gameplan is similar to the Be2 variation.

rn3rk1/pbpPq1pp/1p3n2/5p2/2P5/P1B2N2/1P2.text:
Supposing White takes, this can get really crazy, and not to White's benefit!

...Rad8 is coming!

rn3rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pq2/5p2/2PP4/P1PBPN2/5.text: And here I like ...Qf6 to begin getting some activity on the kingside and to counter White's plans in the center with my own activity.

rnbq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/3P1p2/2P5/P1B2N2.text:
8.d5 occurs 7% of the time but it's a thematic move in the Dutch, so we have to look at it.

I mentioned that this pawn break was one of White's goals, but it's important that White achieve this under better circumstances.

In this particular Dutch, without a knight on c6 and with the light-squared bishop going to b7, d5 lacks force.

rnbq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2NBPN2.text:
White here usually plays Bd3 to fight for control of e4.

We should fianchetto.

rnbq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B1PN2.text:
8.e3 is played 64% of the times here. 

That's why I said that 6. e3 could transpose into 6.a3, because this could be the position if White switches the order of these moves. 

White here wants to develop their light-squared bishop.

We should just fianchetto and control e4.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
6.e3 is a natural way of developing. White wants Be2 or d3 to castle kingside.

This occurs at a rate of 44%, but if you remove the transpositions to 6. a3 it probably becomes much rarer than 44%.

We should go for our setup with the fianchetto on the long diagonal.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N2N2/1.text:
6.a3 (played 34% of the time) is not as popular as 6. e3 first, but there's not much of a difference. 

Besides, 6. e3 can often transpose to 6. a3 if White plays a3.

We should just capture. 

Even though we're not ruining the structure, we're still getting more control of the e4-square.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B2N2/1P.text:
White now recaptures.

And now ...b6 to activate our light-squared bishop is best.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP1.text:
A defensive-minded player will go for Bd2, unpinning. 

This is played 21% of the time after 4...Bb4.

I suggest we just castle, since capturing right away on c3, unprovoked, isn't useful with the bishop already on d2.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White goes for the Two Knights setup.

The variation I recommend here is 4...Bb4.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White goes for Nc3.

And we'll connect the pawns on the light squares.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
2.c4 is by far the most popular move. 

We'll activate our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
For this second study, I want us to focus on White's 5.Bd2 move. 

They defend their knight and we have to make a decision about our bishop on b4.

lessons.title: White Plays the 2 Knights Setup (Nc3 + Nf3)  with 5.e3 or 5.a3

r2q1rk1/pbpn2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P1PBP.text:
And all our pieces are out with good squares.

...e5 is a move we can aspire to, but it would be useful to prepare it with a multipurpose move like ...Qe8.

Remember there are some fork possibilities if we are able to play ...e5.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P1PBP.text:
White should play 9. Bd3 because Be2 would be too passive, giving away full control of e4.

We are going to develop.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/B1PBPN2.text:
White may attempt putting their bishop to good use.

And 9...Re8 is good here, rather than ...d6, when White can play c5 with a good position.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2NBPN2/.text:
White castles.

We've already fianchettoed, we're about to castle, and the pin isn't on the board anymore, so we should damage the structure while we can.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P1P1PN.text:
White plays e3 freely, since the bishop isn't behind the pawn chain.

Castling is fine here.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/2PBPN2/P.text:
White recaptures.

And I think castling is fine here.

rn1qr1k1/p1pp2pp/4p3/2B2p2/3Pb3/2P1PN2/P.text:
Our light-squared bishop will have a strong diagonal and activity for the entire game to come. 

We're going to play with ...d6 and ...Nd7. 

A potential ...Rb8 would also be good to control the b-file, and the position is about equal.

rn1qr1k1/pbp3pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2PP4/B1PBPN2.text:
We now control c5 and will follow up with ...Nbd7. 

We also control the e4-square, which we can make use of soon enough. 

We have a very strong center thanks to the e4-square we can use as a pivot.

rn1qr1k1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/2P2p2/3P4/B1PBPN.text:
c5 could also be played right now, but not to great effect.

I like just taking the pawn, encouraging White to either double their pawns or move their bishop yet again.

rn1qr1k1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/B1PBPN2.text: If the slower Re1 is played, I like ...d6, controlling c5.

rn1qr1k1/pbpp2pp/4pn2/2B2p2/3P4/2PBPN2/P.text:
When the bishop recaptures, it can be attacked.

The knight can be centralized, attacking c5.

rnb1k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/P1P2N2/.text: And we'll just recapture, with many of our same ideas as in the first study to come.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N1PN2/.text: This transposes into 5.Bd2 lines, which we saw in Study 1 of this chapter.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2NBPN2/.text:
The d3-square is generally the most desirable square for the bishop in 1.d4 openings. 

However, in the Dutch it stares at our f5-pawn.

We should increase our control of e4 with ...Bb7.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N1PN2.text: This transposes into 5.a3 lines where e3 is played later.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P1P2N2.text:
This bishop move makes the most sense.

We should fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1P2N2/.text:
This pin recreates the main line we've seen in Study 1 of this chapter, but the useless move a3 has been included.

We should do the same thing we do against it in the main line.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
And now quite simply the move e3, which is played 14% of the time here. 

This move blocks in the c1-bishop, but it's still useful to see because it's quite natural.

We can just wait and make other useful moves before taking. 

Let's see if White wastes a tempo with a3.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N2N2/1P.text:
Some players—nearly 38,000 or 10% of those who have seen this position, to be exact—don't like pins.

But the entire point of ...Bb4 is to take on c3 and damage the pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1P2N2/4PP.text:
White recaptures.

And, consistent with our development scheme in the Dutch, we play ...b6 to fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
And here comes the popular two knights setup.

We'll continue with the pin like in the previous study.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
The white knight goes to c3. This is the most popular third move.

3...e6 helps defend f5 and control the d5-square.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
2.c4 is by far the most popular move, getting the d- and c-pawns into action.

And we'll develop our knight to the f6-square, as will be common in this course.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study of the Gotham Dutch, we will be seeing the same two knights setup but instead of bishop moves on move 5, we will see pawn moves. 

5.e3 and 5.a3 are somewhat popular; however, they are not the most critical ways White has of playing. We should have an easy middlegame if we follow some simple recommendations.

2bqk2r/1ppp2pp/2n1pn2/rQ3p2/p1PP4/P1N2N2.text: It can be won. Good game.

r1bqk2r/1ppp2pp/2n1pn2/1Q3p2/p1PP4/P1N2N.text: If the queen goes to b5...

r1bqk2r/1ppp2pp/2n1pn2/2Q2p2/p1PP4/P1N2N.text:
On c5, the queen isn't safe at all.

8...b6 is the simplest.

r1bqk2r/2pp2pp/1pn1pn2/1Q3p2/p1PP4/P1N2N.text: When the queen goes to its only square...

r4rk1/pbpn2p1/1p1ppq1p/5p2/2PP4/P1Q1PN2/.text:
And now we should develop the knight.  

It's nice to see that we have a solid central formation, being ready to expand with ...f4 and ...e5. 

If the e5-pawn push needs support,  ...Rae8 could be played.

rn1q1rk1/pbp3pp/1p1ppn2/2P2p2/3P4/B1P2NP.text:
So let's say that c5 is played now...

We can capture.

rn1q1rk1/pbp3pp/1p2pn2/2P2p2/8/B1P2NP1/P.text:
And when White recaptures...

We can move our rook onto a safe square.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/B1P2NP1.text:
9.Ba3 can lead to some interesting play, but it's similar to a Ba3 variation we've seen in this chapter already (see the 5.e3 line).

The difference here is that we can play ...d6 because the pawn moves don't come with the same pressure.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2P2NP1.text:
We've already explored White's Bg5 ideas against our Dutch.

The solution is the same here. We push the bishop away or force it to take.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2p1/1p2pB1p/5p2/2PP4/P1Q2N2/.text:
And to avoid ...Ne4 many people take.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/2P2NP1/P.text:
White castles.

And we can castle as well.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1Q2N2/.text:
This pins is one of the most reasonable attempts from White, also seeking to prevent ...Ne4 with a tempo on the queen.

We should kick the bishop out.

rn1qr1k1/1bp3pp/1p2pn2/5p2/8/B1P2NP1/P3P.text:
In fact, we are the ones who get a semi-open a-file with pressure on White's pieces.

White will have permanent weaknesses on c3 and a2 that it will be our job to target in the middlegame.

rn1qr1k1/pbp3pp/1P2pn2/5p2/8/B1P2NP1/P3P.text: But in all of this, White doesn't get anything special.

rn2k2r/pbp3p1/1p1ppq1p/5p2/1bPP4/2N1PN2/.text:
We have ideas of ...c5 to expand in the center. 

...g5 is a strong idea to gain kingside space, making White uncomfortable. 

After that, a good question for White will be where they should castle. 

If White unpins the knight or plays a3, taking on c3 with the bishop will be forced.

rn2k2r/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/1bPP4/2N1PN2/.text:
9.Be2 is a solid looking move that reinforces the knight on f3. 

Some players may worry that you may want to take on f3 and double yet another pair of pawns.

rn2k2r/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/P1Q1PN2/.text:
e3 is a consistent pawn move across this course.

We can get our king to safety.

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P2NP1/P.text:
We recapture.

We want to continue our development with ...Be4 and ...Nc6. 

A trade of bishops on g2 will be a neutral trade for us, or even beneficial since it's a piece that defends White's king.

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/P1Q1PN2/.text:
Be2 lends the knight some support.

...d6 is played to control e5 and to develop, as per usual.

rnb1k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/1bPP4/2N1PN2.text:
You may see White continue with 8.e3 to open up their bishop.

Let's just fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/1ppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/p1PP4/P1Q2N2/1P.text: This is the third queen move in the opening.

rnbqk2r/1ppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/pQPP4/P1N2N2/1P.text:
Many players take the piece thinking it's free.

But it simply isn't free.

We can attack the queen.

rnbqk2r/1ppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/pbPP4/P1N2N2/1P.text:
Because of the traps, Qc2 should be played.

When we capture the knight, we have already improved our position a lot.

rnbqk2r/1ppp2pp/4pn2/p4p2/1bPP4/PQN2N2/1.text:
The move 6.a3 doesn't achieve our immediate withdrawal or capture of the knight. 

We can go for a trap.

Playing a4 forces the queen back!

rnbqk2r/2pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/p1PP4/P1Q2N2/1.text:
And we stand quite better with the because our advanced a-pawn controls both of White's queenside pawns. 

White could continue with moves like e3 and Be2 or g3 and Bg2, or even Bg5, in which case you know ...h6 is good. 

After we develop with ...Bb7 and castle, we can go ...Ne4 and ...Rf6, keeping an eye on the g5-square.

rnbqk2r/p1p5/1p1ppn1p/5pp1/2PP4/2P2NB1/P.text:
And now we're going to continue with ...Qe7, which will force White to make room to save their bishop.

White has ideas of e3 and 0-0-0, so the game could continue with 10.e3 Qe7 11.0-0-0 Nbd7. 

But your plan is to develop and just enjoy the fact you have more space and a better structure.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pB1p/5p2/1bPP4/2N2N2/.text:
White now takes, usually.

And we recapture, activating our queen.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pn1p/5p2/1bPP3B/2N2N2.text:
But going to h4 for White is now rather possible.

This expansion is still good for us.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N2N2/.text:
6.a3 forces Black to a decision here.

We should be consistent and take, making White move their queen again.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/2P2NP1/P.text:
White fianchettoes.

And so do we.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1Q2N2/1.text:
White recaptures with the queen, keeping their structure intact.

We should fianchetto as we are used to doing.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/2N2N2/.text:
If White pins you, we'll react the same way we do in Study 1 and 2.

We will attack the g5-bishop to get rid of the pin.

rnbqk2r/p1pp4/1p2pn1p/5pp1/1bPP4/2N2NB1/.text:
The bishop goes to g3. 

But unlike Study 1, there's a queen on c2 that could give a check if we move the f-pawn!

We can insert the capture on c3 here. White mustn't recapture with the queen, as they need to retain the option of Qg6+.

rnbqk2r/p1pp4/1p2pn1p/5pp1/2PP4/2P2NB1/P.text: So White has to get doubled pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/1QN2N2/PP.text:
The other queen move is Qb3, both attacking the bishop and defending the knight.

It's played only 4% of the time.

In this position, 5...a5 defends the bishop but also starts setting up some traps.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N2N2/PPQ.text:
Let's explore the queen moves first. 

5.Qc2 defends the knight to recapture with the queen and avoid wrecking the structure.

5.Qc2 is played 7% of the time here. But it's a really natural move for 1.d4 players, similar to the Capablanca Variation of the Nimzo for example.

And here we should just go ...b6, as we're in no rush to take on c3.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
Finally, 5.g3 occurs 6% of the time, but you could indeed see it because it's a very natural way to play for White in other Dutch variations. 

The point is that the bishop on g2 reinforces future e4- or d5-pawn pushes.

Since the knight wasn't defended, we should go ahead and double the pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2P2NP1/P3P.text:
White recaptures.

And we want to get on the diagonal at the same time that White establishes their bishop on g2 or we may not get the chance.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White goes for the Two Knights setup, as we've seen.

And after we go for this pin, there are some sidelines that are worth exploring because they are not bad.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White develops their knight.

We connect our pawns.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White activates their pawn duo.

We develop the knight and control e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
I hope that from the previous studies, you have an overall feel of what playing the Gotham Dutch entails. 

We can summarize it into controlling the e4-square and attacking on the kingside, but we can also be positional, by doubling White's pawns on the c-file in this Two Knights variation. 

Let's see what happens if White plays a queen move or g3 on move 5.

r1bq1rk1/p1pn4/1p1ppn1p/5pp1/2PP4/2PBPNB.text:
I advise we play here first. That's because if d5 now, ...Nc5 refutes it.

We can now go ...Bb7 without a care in the world, and if White tries d5 they'll give up the c5-square. 

...Qe7 can be played to connect the rooks.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2PBP.text:
White puts their knight on e2, but it isn't the best piece there.

Many of the squares to which it could go are either occupied or could be occupied by another White piece.

We can now x-ray the queen.

r2q1rk1/pbp3pp/1pnppn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2PBP1Q.text:
Hence we can block that diagonal.

White needs to be careful about ...Nh5. 

We've also got neat ideas of ...Qe8 and ...e5 to expand in the center. 

Somehow, White has a worse position out of the opening.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2PBP1.text:
It is very probable that White gets off the diagonal immediately. 

This attacks c7.

r3k2r/pbpp2p1/1pn1pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPQ2/P.text:
But now our bishop x-rays the queen.

We're going to castle kingside and play for ...e5. 

White isn't prepared to deal with our piece and pawn activity. The queen on f3 isn't ideally placed and White will likely have to waste a move repositioning it.

rn3rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBP3/P3.text:
And now we castle as well. 

We'll go ...d6 and we have an idea of ...Nc6 to a5, since the knight is quite safe on that dark square.

rnb1k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBP3/P.text:
Only Nc3 setups require that your opponent doesn't go to f3 with the knight.

But at this point we can just control the diagonal and exert great pressure.

rnb1k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBPQ2/.text:
If the queen comes out, always remember this is a superficial plan from White.

In the longer term, we will gain the tempo back.

rnb1k2r/p1pp2p1/1p2pq1p/5p2/2PP4/P1P1P3/.text:
Our bishop will pose some problems. 

We've already seen that Qf3 in positions like this isn't a good move: ...Nc6 and ...Bb7 threaten the f3-queen. 

Resisting the transposition into Nf3 ideas is hard for White and so, on the off-chance that this does happen, you should have a comfortable advantage with moves like ...Bb7 and ...Nc6.

rnb1k2r/ppp3p1/3ppq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P1P1P1/P.text:
Against g3 I suggest we adopt a setup with ...d6, and prepare an eventual ...e5.

We cannot get our queenside fianchetto, so we'll instead develop and prepare our thematic pawn break with ...e5.

This position will end up being quite good for us because we'll be controlling many squares with our e5- and f5-pawns.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/1bPP4/2N5/PPQ1.text: We can recapture, with all our traditional Dutch moves coming up next: ...b6 for ...Bb7, ...d6 for ...Nd7 and ...0-0.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2P1P1P1/P.text: One of the unique moves that you could see is 8.g3.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/2PP4/2PBP3/P4P.text:
Putting the bishop on d3 doesn't transpose back to anything, unless of course White plays their knight to f3.

But this allows us to play our traditional queenside fianchetto.

rnbq1k1r/pppp4/4pnQp/6p1/1bPP1p2/2N3B1/P.text:
And White runs out of ideas.

We will win the bishop on g3 next move.

rnbq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2PBPQ.text:
Some players may jump at the sight of the open diagonal and want to gain a tempo.

But it is Black who will win a tempo by putting a bishop opposite the queen!

9.d5 isn't a problem because of 9...Na5 and we can still go 10...Bb7.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3p1/3ppn1p/5p2/2PP3B/2PBPN2/.text:
The bishop comes out to d3. 

Perhaps White intends to support the e4-pawn push.

If that's the case, I like 9...g5 here because this implies that our knight will be kept on f6, fighting for the e4-square. 

We break the pin and ensure our knight's stability for the time being.

rnbq1rk1/ppp5/3ppn1p/5pp1/2PP4/2PBPNB1/P.text:
The bishop has to go back.

And now 10...b6 is in the spirit of everything we've been learning thus far. 

But I don't think we can play ...Bb7 so fast here because of the bishop on d3.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5p2/2PP3B/2P1PN2/.text:
White may now develop to f3.

We should cover the e5-square.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2PBP3/P.text:
The bishop is brought out to d3.

The bishop is usually good on this square, but against the Dutch that becomes debatable.

And our setup works even now without Nf3 on the board.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pB1p/5p2/1bPP4/2N5/PPQ1.text: We're already accustomed to positions where White captures on f6.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pB1p/5p2/2PP4/2P1P3/P4P.text:
If White takes, we're happy to see them give the bishop pair up so quickly.

We can recapture with the queen as we often do.

Like I've said, 8.Nf3 or Nf3 in general will likely transpose back to chapter 1.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pB1p/5p2/2PP4/P1P5/4PPP.text:
White takes, and we recapture.

This doesn't make the most sense for White since we both gave up our bishops, but only one side has doubled pawns. 

Black is better. This may transpose into Chapter 1 after 8.Nf3 and 8...b6.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5p2/1bPP3B/2N5/PPQ.text:
If the bishop goes to h4, we can trap it.

Pretty much, whenever you see e3 hasn't been played, trapping the bishop should come to mind.

6...g5 attacks it.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5p2/2PP3B/2P1P3/P4.text:
White could choose to play Bh4 because we cannot trap it on g3 after they have played e3, helping control the f4-square.

I suggest we simply castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
You will probably face 5.e3, as it is the natural idea after 4. Bf4.

And here I suggest we double the pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2P1P3/P4.text:
White recaptures.

And we've managed to both castle and control the center before move 7. 

This is a win in my book!

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
5.e3 is the most popular move at 27% played by 50,000 + people in the database, and it's a natural move as well.

Once again, we're going to take on c3 and double the pawns.

The reason we take right away here is that if we wait by playing 5...b6, 6.Qb3 attacks our bishop and defends the knight.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/2N5/PPQ1.text:
Finally, the queen could defend c3.

We should attack the bishop and try to get White to trade it off.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/P1N5/1P2.text:
White could immediately just push and force the bishop away. 

Some players claim that having the bishop pair is good enough compensation for the doubled pawns.

We should accept this offer from them.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2P1P3/P4P.text:
White recaptures.

And after doubling the pawns, we'll ask White how exactly they intend to keep their bishop pair.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1P5/4PPP.text:
The pawn recaptures.

Basically, we always want to go ...h6 when we see the bishop on g5.

We don't have to double up our pawns to recapture, as we can develop our queen instead.

rnbqk2r/pppp4/4pn1p/5pp1/1bPP4/2N3B1/PPQ.text:
When it goes to g3...

We don't mind the check on g6.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2N5/PP2.text:
This move is played 7% of the time here, but the sample size is still large.

White wants to control the e5-square like in the London and they want their bishop out before e3 is played.

We'll go ahead and pin.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2N5/PP2P.text:
And 29% of the time, White plays 4.Bg5, going for the pin right away.

We don't have to fix what isn't broken.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
And this move occurs 70% of the time after d4 and c4, with the ideas I mentioned in the previous chapter.

They are controlling e4 and supporting future pawn breaks on light squares.

Our moves are not to be changed: we're going to open up our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White activates their pawn duo.

We develop our knight and control e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 2! 

We will continue looking at the Dutch, but instead of both knights coming out, you may also face only Nc3 early on. 

3.Nc3 is a very common third move from White in the Dutch, and it's thematic, so you could possibly see it without Nf3. 

Let's see how this leads to slightly different positions than in the previous chapter.

r1b2rk1/pp1p2pp/n2Qpn2/q1P2p2/2P5/2P1P1P.text:
They won't be able to defend it for long. 

Black has a long-term strategic advantage due to the better structure; I should say that in most cases we want to take on c5 with the knight. 

The queen is fine where it is, with pressure on c3. ...Nxc5 should be next because it also supports ...Nfe4.

r1bq1rk1/pp1p2pp/n2Qpn2/2P2p2/2P5/2P1P1P.text: For example if White defends c5...

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PPn3/P1B2NP1/.text:
The other knight comes to support its partner. 

We have now blocked the h1-a8 diagonal and enabled ...b6 for ...Bb7. 

...Qe7 should also be played to connect the rooks and your position should be solid out of the opening.

r1bq1rk1/pppn2pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B2NP1/.text:
If we do see this knight coming out to f3, now we can jump into e4 without it being captured.

This threatens to double the pawns.

r2q1rk1/pbpn2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2PP4/P1BBPP2.text:
After they castle...

We can bring our queen into e7 and we have connected rooks.

r2q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/2nP1p2/2PN4/P1P3P.text:
But our knight is in a great outpost and it helps defend e6. 

From here we can play ...Bd6 and ...Qe7. 

Our knight could even contemplate going to e4 since if the bishop takes it we'll be the ones with a strong bishop pair.

r2q1rk1/pbppb1pp/np2p3/3P1p2/2PN4/P1P3P1.text: White centralizes their knight, which attacks e6.

r4rk1/pbpnq1pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/1PPP4/P1BBPP2.text: Even here after the rather natural and engine-approved 12.b4, I believe we can still prepare ...e5.

r4rk1/pbpnq2p/1p1ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/P1BBPP2.text:
One possible idea is ...e5 and if the queen ever goes to c2, we even threaten ...e4 to trap the bishop. 

If the d-file opens up after trades, ...Rad8 will be a great move that will pose practical problems and White is starting to run out of natural good moves. 

Only engine-like precision is what remains for White to keep the advantage.

rn1q1rk1/pbp3pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2PP4/P1BBPP2.text:
White gets their knight out.

And we do the same.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1BBPP2.text:
9.Bd3 is the best developing move at this point, but some people do make the inaccurate 9.Ne2, blocking the bishop in. 

We should make use of ...d6 to develop the knight to d7 rather than c6 where it blocks our bishop.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/3P1p2/2P5/P1P2NP.text:
10.d5 controls our c6-square, so our knight cannot be placed there.

But it also attacks our e6-pawn, so we cannot play ...d6.

That's why we have to go to a6. 

Our knight will have a great outpost on c5. This is a consequence of White pushing forward with 10.d5.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5pB1/2PPn3/P1NBP.text:
And now we can jump into e4 and open up an attack on the g5-bishop. 

Most likely you'll see trades here. A possible continuation is 9.Bxe7 Qxe7 10.0-0 c5. 

Once ...c5 is on the board, the maneuver ...Nc6 to a5 is logical.

And we centralize our knight which cannot easily be taken. 

Once again, just like we've seen, this will probably result in trades that leave Black with an open f-file and a developed queen.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B1PP2/.text:
8.f3 is a great move, as it counters what I mentioned was our biggest advantage: the light squares!

But it's not like White is winning already, as they are behind in development.

We are castled and have developed two minor pieces, while they aren't castled and only have a bishop on c3.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PP4/P1P2NP1/.text:
White recaptures.

We can now castle. 

d5 isn't the biggest of issues because we've already traded off the c3-knight.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/P1N2NP1.text:
White can castle here.

And now we can double their pawns.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1N2NP1.text:
White gets their bishop into the diagonal.

White will play d5 and they'll disconnect our bishop from the e4-square if we don't play ...Ne4 now.

Our idea is to trade the c3-knight, anticipating d5. If Nxe4, ...Bxe4 and our bishop won't be blocked in with d5.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1N1PN.text:
You should expect White to go ahead and connect their pawns.

Our development continues as normal. 

We should castle and get ready to jump our knight into e4.

Few moves make independent sense for White. 

They'll probably have to go back to our Chapter 1 with the Two Knights setup.

We should therefore just castle.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1N2NP1.text:
One option for White is to contest the long diagonal.

e7 is the best square for us. 

We want to avoid ...Bd6 because of Nb5 ideas.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1N1P3.text:
White goes 6.e3 to connect their pawns.

Most of the times, we've played ...h6 to get rid of the pin. 

But this time, I feel ...Be7 is fine because e7 is our bishop's best square now after 4.a3.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1N2N2.text:
White could go for the pin at this moment.

We should just unpin with our bishop, since we have to play it to e7 either way.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p2pp/4pn2/2P2p2/2P5/2P1P1P1/.text:
Taking on c5 isn't ideal, but d5 wouldn't have been either.

We can continue the development of our pieces around the clumsy queenside tripled pawns.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/3ppn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N3P1/1.text:
7.a3 is usually played to resolve the situation on the queenside.

We should just capture.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B3P1/1P.text:
White recaptures with their bishop.

And now we have a plan to control the e4-square.

We're going to jump the knight in there and support it with the other knight.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N1P1P1/.text:
6.e3 is common at this point. 

But this allows us to double the pawns.

We take.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N3P1/PP.text:
White could also find it reasonable to want to recapture on c3 with their bishop to avoid damaging the pawns.

As long as there's a piece that can be taken in the next move on c3 or d2, we should just continue developing. 

If 7.Qb3, 7...c5 or ...a5 are ideas.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2P1P1P1/P.text:
White recaptures. 

We have a structural advantage, but we do want to be careful about our b7-pawn.

I like how ...c5 looks here, as it enables our queen's development while also posing problems for White's center.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N1P3/.text:
The thing is that our dark-squared bishop is a problem piece, and the best course of action is to take the knight on c3 and control the e4-square some more.

We should take, despite this not doubling any pawns.

Nonetheless, our control of the light squares is a great plus.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1B1P3/1.text:
The bishop recaptures. 

I must say that this procedure does take some more time for White, so it's not something that's super intuitive.

We should just fianchetto and get our bishop on that beautiful grip of the light squares.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N1P3/PP1.text:
White defends the knight 27% of the time.

This is somewhat problematic since many of those ideas with doubling pawns on the c-file aren't applicable anymore. 

We should just pursue development instead. White's bishop isn't going anywhere.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
5.Bg2 is the natural continuation of 4.g3. 

And now we should just castle and not capture on c3 right away.

rnbqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1N2N2/.text:
Let's say that the other knight comes out to f3.

We can just fianchetto. 

Our bishop generally wants to go to b7 since we have a long light- squared pawn chain that blocks it in.

rnbqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P1N5/1.text:
Such White moves generally occur but when they do so isn't an exact science. 

Some players may go for the pin right away. This transposes to 5.Nf3 and 6.Bg5.

Let's get our bishop into b7 first, and only then will we deal with the pin.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
Now 4.e3 is played 12% of times, but at such an early stage the sample size is quite large and it represents more than 300,000 games in the database. 

We can still go for the pin.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
Next in line in popularity we have 4.g3, going for the kingside fianchetto to try and counter our light square dominion.

It's played 9% of the time.

We can go for the pin to be consistent with our repertoire.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1N5/1P2P.text:
White places a great emphasis on their knight's placement on c3, and a3 is only chosen 2% of the time.

They don't want to deal with the pin, and they also know that the dark-squared bishop is hard to develop and make useful.

Despite this, 4.a3 isn't the fastest move. We can start developing another piece.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White now enters the 3.Nc3 setup again.

We connect our pawns and get some control over d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White goes for their very popular two pawns setup.

We develop our knight and control e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this second study, I think you can see a certain pattern by now: White usually plays the moves e3, g3 or a3 at many different points in the opening. 

We'll focus on White going for these moves early on at move 4 in the 3.Nc3 only setup. 

That way, you won't ever be surprised by these moves!

r2qk2r/pppb2pp/2n5/5p2/1bP1n3/2N1P3/PPQ2.text:
8.e3 covers the d4-square.

But we can add another attacker on c3!

r3k2r/pppb2pp/2n2q2/5p2/1bP1n3/2N1P3/PPQ.text: Pretty much the only idea for White to defend here is 9.Bd2.

r3k2r/pppb2pp/2n2q2/5p2/1bP5/2N1P3/PPQn1.text:
But we can take that bishop right away or we could even go for long castling first. 

The idea to get compensation is similar: ...0-0-0 to put the rook on the d-file, attack the queen with ...Be6, and taking on c3 to double the pawns, even if it means trading queens.

rn1qk2r/pppb2pp/8/5p2/1bP1n3/2N5/PP1BPPP.text:
White has a knight on c3 problem. 

They have to defend it somehow. Breaking the pin with the bishop is often played.

But we should take on c3.

rn1qk2r/pppb2pp/8/5p2/1bP1n3/2N5/PPQ1PPP.text:
7.Qc2 is another way of defending the knight on c3.

But the queen on c2 can come under fire.

rn1qk2r/pppb2pp/8/5p2/2P1n3/2B5/PP2PPPP/.text:
White recaptures.

We continue taking on c3.

rn2k2r/pppb2pp/5q2/5p2/2P5/2P5/P3PPPP/R2.text:
And at the end of all of this, sure, White is a pawn up. But White's c-pawns are doubled and we'll put pressure on them! 

If 10.Qd4, we obviously won't trade queens, but we'll play 10...Qe7 and ...Nc6. 

Since we have an open d-file, we can also look to castle queenside and catch the king in the center of the board!

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/6B1/2PPp3/P1P5/5PP.text:
We can just castle. 

We'll continue with ...h6 and ...Nc6.

White is advised not to take on f6, but play Be3 to support the f2-pawn.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1Q5/1P2.text:
And I think development for us is pretty self-explanatory. 

Do recall that if White develops with 7.Nf3 now, after 7...Bb7 we've transposed into Chapter 1, Study 3. And in my opinion there aren't many rational ways of avoiding this. 

Even if 7.Bg5 first, we'd go 7...h6 and after exchanges on f6 we'll most likely see Nf3 at some point.

rnbqk2r/pppP2pp/8/5p2/1bP1n3/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
Continuing to take pawns just speeds up our development. 

A pawn is a small price to pay for a big attack!

We should recapture with the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4Pn2/5p2/1bP5/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Some players, thinking that they're losing their grip on d5, will take on e6 and try to damage your pawns.

But as a result Black gets a massive initiative!

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P1N5/1PQ1.text:
5.a3 is the most common idea now. 

Since the queen is already on c2, White often thinks it good to force the trade. They will recapture with the queen either way.

We should just go ahead and take, since doubling the pawns isn't the only idea behind ...Bb4.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1Q5/1P2PP.text: White recaptures with their queen and they keep their pawns healthy.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/6B1/1bPPp3/P1N5/1P3.text:
If White simply wants to get rid of the pin...

We'll happily grant them this much and capture.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/6B1/2PPp3/P1P5/5PPP.text: When they recapture, now their pawns are doubled and they no longer attack e4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p4/2PPP3/2N5/PP4PP.text: If White tries to take and claim that our pawns are weak, we will prove to them that winning the pawn back isn't simple.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/8/2PPp3/2N5/PP4PP/R.text:
We'll just recapture, and believe it or not, the pin on the c3-knight will come with devastating effect. 

The only way I could think of that White may try to stop it is 7.a3. But that's already an admission of fear in a player that just went for a gambit. 

...Nc6 will put pressure on d4 and we'll castle, getting a better position as White attempts to win the pawn back.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/2N5/PP2P.text:
Finally, 4.d5 is played 1% of times, having been played around 100,000 times in the database. 

Seeing this occur so early in the game is rare, probably because it doesn't have enough support.

Let's first pin one of its most important defenders.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PPQ1P.text:
Qc2 is a very natural move amongst 1.d4 players: the queen defends the knight and helps prepare an e4-pawn push. 

At move 4, Qc2 occurs 3% of the time, but at this stage this represents over 100,000 games.

And because we're focused on development, we'll bring this bishop out and pin the knight, also gaining some more control over e4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PPP3/2N5/PP3P.text:
First, 4.e4 could be attempted. 

Maybe White wants to play in gambit style or they are optimistic thinking they can win it back. 

This occurs a mere 3% of the time, but I don't want you to be taken by surprise.

Let's just take with the pawn. If  Qe2, ...d5 will be our response.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/6B1/2PPp3/2N5/PP3P.text:
This move is more common than 5.f3, but it's worse.

It just allows the pin right away. 

Nothing White plays will prevent the capture on c3, removing the e4-pawn's attacker.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/8/2PPp3/2N2P2/PP4P.text:
5.f3 is the best attempt for White to try and prove that they're playing a gambit.

5...d5 will be the most commonly played move in this variation. The idea is to defend the e4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White plays their knight out to c3 where it helps the pawns in their control of the center.

And we connect our pawn chain and get ready to develop the dark-squared bishop. 

Let's begin by seeing White's pawn breaks being played really early on.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White gets their pawns working together.

We develop, controlling e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this last study, we're going to explore some branches after 3.Nc3 that have to do with mostly pawn moves, but we'll also see a classical queen move. 

The first two pawn moves aren't at all that challenging for Black. 

And 4.Qc2 isn't tough to face, but it's solid. Let's see what to do against them.

r4rk1/p1pp2pp/1pn1pq2/5p2/2PPb3/5NP1/PP1.text:
But we've developed everything and connected the rooks. 

It's hard to give White a plan to make their advantage grow. We can go for an ...h6 and ...g5 expansion in the meantime. 

Moves like ...Ne7 and ...Rf7 are small ideas that we can employ to get our pieces a bit closer to the kingside where we may attack if White isn't careful.

rn1q1rk1/1bpp2pp/1p2pn2/p4p2/2PP4/PP3NP1.text:
White may therefore elect b3 to develop their bishop.

And now I suggest you develop your queen. 

We are going to get a harmonious setup out of the opening like we're used to at this point.

rn1q1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPb3/2Q2NP1/.text:
But we can centralize this strong bishop to make it harder for White to block us in with d5 ideas.

After this, development could be moves like ...Qf6, ...d6 and ...Nd7.

rn1q1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPb3/5NP1/PP.text:
A good player will know that they must activate their rook, and they'll seek to avoid the trade of bishops. 

But by no means does it mean that your opponent won't try stuff like 11.Ne5 and simply allow 11...Bxg2, making your life easier.

At any rate, against best play, we should just continue being principled and develop our pieces.

rn1q1rk1/pbp3pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1.text:
And we're getting ready to develop our knight and our queen, connecting the rooks.

We can move our queen to the side onto a light square to control this color complex a lot more.

Our knight has many options, but d7 is a safe one, after which we could play for a move like ...c5.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PP4/2Q2NP1/P.text: The queen recaptures to maintain the integrity of the pawn chain.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPN3/5NP1/PP.text:
Taking on e4 is the most natural response.

And we recapture with our bishop. 

Our entire point is that our bishop cannot be blocked with d5 pushes and if the knight moves we'll get even more trades in.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/2N2NP1/.text:
Another natural response is simply moving the queen away and not capturing on Black's terms.

But I think all trades are on our terms. 

We want to trade pieces since we have less space to move around and our development isn't complete.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P4NP1/.text:
If a3 now, then we are forced to take because our position is quite cramped. 

Proof of this is that both the queen and bishop could make use of the e7-square. So, with less space, it's advantageous to trade pieces.

We should take.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
Now, Nc3 is expected since the queen is on d2.

And I really like this move at this point, clarifying the situation on the board and getting more trades in.

If we can guarantee some trades, it'll be more difficult for White to successfully attack us.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP.text: White can go to the c2-square with their queen.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1.text:
Catalan players like to play g3, Nf3 and castles in as much of a sequential order as possible.

And recall how I said b4 was an idea?  If White doesn't play it, we can go ...a5 to gain space.

Had White played this move before, we could also respond with ...a5, undermining the pawn.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/5NP1/PP.text:
White castles. Primarily, this unpins the knight on d2.

However, we're in no rush to take it. 

The logic behind this is that it doesn't have anywhere useful to go.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP1.text:
White may castle.

But we can do the same as well.

White castles. And we can do the same. 

Notice how we still have the tempo on the queen but we haven't gone ahead and played it. 

This gives us the chance of trading bishops if the f3-knight moves.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1P.text:
White now gets their bishop on g2, but since the structure isn't a traditional d4/d5, locked pawn chain, the traditional "Catalan Bishop" doesn't do much damage.

We can castle.

White can get on the long diagonal now as well.

And we can castle.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P5P1/1P1.text:
Here, we quite simply gain a tempo on the h1-rook. White has to go back to f3 and all they've done is lost time.

...0-0, ...d6 and ...Nbd7 will be our moves. Black has equalized.

rn3rk1/1bp1q1pp/1p1ppn2/p4p2/2PP4/PP3NP1.text:
And we can start getting ready to develop our knight. 

That ...Ne4 tempo we kept in store all this time could be of us to us soon in this middlegame. 

Another tip is that if White goes d5 at some point we'll want to trade with ...exd5 most of the time. 

Blocking our own bishop on b7 by locking down the pawns wouldn't be the ideal.

rn3rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pq2/5p2/2PPb3/5NP1/PP1.text: White could go for something like this, centralizing at last both of their rooks.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PPQ.text:
And we can go to e7. 

White may go for a d5-pawn push. But we want to go ...Nbd7 and prepare ...e5, which, to be fair, could be tough to play because of the queen's pressure on f5.

...c5 could be an idea, but in the video I try to explore the dynamics of this position a lot more, since White can do many different things.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/5NP1/PP.text:
Most of the time, you'll see Bg2, since it's only natural to pair the movement of these b- or g-pawns with a fianchetto.

We should do the same to avoid any tactics on our rook.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P4NP1/1.text:
White may argue that they're getting the bishop pair and that this trade will help them develop.

And, in a way, they are right. 

But this trade helps us develop, too.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP1.text:
White enters the g2-square.

But we get on the h1-a8 diagonal just in time.

White gets their bishop into g2.

We hop into the light squares as well.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1P.text:
By far the most natural and best move is to recapture with the bishop.

We should get on the long diagonal.

Without a knight on c3, our control of the light squares is vastly superior.

Recapturing with the queen comes with the downside of also blocking the c1-bishop, so perhaps White will have to resort to b4 and Bb2.

Another downside is that we can play ...Ne4 at any moment. But we  should keep this threat in our pocket and just develop our pieces.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P5P1/1P1.text:
And finally, this recapture moves the knight away from the center. 

It's hard to see how the knight is better on d2 than on f3.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
Finally if this is played, suddenly we're back into Chapter 1 because the two knights are out.

And it's played 15% of the time.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/5NP1/PP1B.text:
Blocking with the bishop allows us to trade, and thus no player can claim a bishop pair advantage.

It's played 72% of the time.

We'll gladly capture.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/5NP1/PP1N.text:
Blocking with the knight temporarily impedes White's piece development, and White players opt for this move 13% of the time.

The knight blocks the c1-bishop.

Since we've already gained our tempo and developed, it's time to develop something else!

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP1NP.text:
White recaptures with their knight 75% of the time.

We should just proceed with our plan to activate our bishop on its best diagonal.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP1QP.text:
Taking with the queen is less common, and it allows us a tempo deeper into the middlegame when it is more convenient.

We should first develop and not attack the queen just because we can. 

Remember that White's bishop is coming into g2 and ...b6 would be hard to get later.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
And this is the part where White may go for light square control, as they play g3 17% of the time.

Let's play an inbetween move before we develop the light-squared bishop!  

This move speeds up our development because it comes with a check and it forces White to play into something they may not want.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
3.Nf3 is played 11% of the times, but this percentage corresponds to more than 600,000 games. 

We should expect White to develop one or both of their knights in the opening, regardless of the order.

We should now continue with the move that prepares the development of our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White puts the two pawns in the center.

We should play 2...Nf6 now, as we have been doing.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to this third chapter on the Gotham Dutch. 

As you've probably noticed by now, we've covered the Two Knights, then White only playing Nc3, and now White only playing Nf3. 

This first study will focus on what to play against players that go for a Catalan. When White goes g3, they get on the diagonal that we also want to get on. Let's see how to fight this!

r2q1rk1/pbpn2pp/1p1pp3/5p2/2PPnB2/P3PN2/.text:
We have a pretty solid position because our d6- and c7-pawns block the bishop on f4. 

We're going to continue with ...g5 and even ...c5 for our main pawn pushes, and we'll also seek to go for a kingside attack if possible. 

After ...g5 has been played and if it is safe, we can also take our d7-knight to f6.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPnB2/P3PN2/.text:
The queen moves away. 

This wasn't just a one move threat. It was a centralization of our knight.

And now we can blunt the bishop's diagonal and clear a path for our knight.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P3PN2.text:
White develops their bishop to castle.

And now is a good time to go for this tempo.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P3PN2/.text:
We should just castle here. 

White could prepare d5 at some point. If they do, that'll give us the c5-square, so we can go for something like ...Na6-c5.  

In general, we want to unpin with ...Qe8 and we can even make use of e4 with ...Be4 or ...Ne4.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P3PN2/.text:
White pushes 8.e3 and connects their pawns.

I suggest we castle. 

Our development is going smoothly after the bishop trade on d2, which is exactly why we went for it.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P3PN2/1.text:
8.e3, connecting the pawns and getting ready to develop the light-squared bishop, is the most White can do with the e-pawn. 

Our control of e4 cannot be easily challenged.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/P4N2/.text:
White commonly forces us to take on d2.

And we will take because we don't have that much space for our bishop.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P4N2/1.text:
White recaptures with their queen, arguing that they're developing a piece. 

But this gives us a future tempo with ...Ne4.

We want to fianchetto and get all our pieces into their best squares before we go forward to attack the queen.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/P4N2/1.text:
If White pressures you to take...

You'll gladly do so since the bishop doesn't have room in your position.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/P4N2/1P.text:
The queen recaptures and White gets another piece out.

But Black's development isn't falling behind at all.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/2N2N2/P.text: This takes us back to Chapter 1.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/5N2/PP1.text:
This is the only logical move that doesn't lead back to Chapter 1.

We should go for our fianchetto here.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP.text: We have seen this in Chapter 1.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/5N2/PP1N.text:
5.Nbd2 is the interposition that doesn't transpose back into the Two Knights Chapter.

5...b6 remains the best way to develop our bishop in these circumstances.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/5N2/PP2.text:
White could get their bishop into f4 in the style of the London.

This occurs 2% of the time, around 30,000+ times in the database.

Against 4.Bf4, we can give the Bb4 check and once again White is faced with the dilemma of not wanting to move their bishop back.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.text:
And going for this pin is quite natural. 

It is also played 12% of the time, occurring about 150,000 times in the database.

But when the bishop leaves c1 like that, this check is all that much more effective. 

Basically, it sort of makes fun of White's last move since if they block with the bishop they've moved that piece twice.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White now develops their king's knight, getting to the Nf3 setup but not completely indicating if they'll go for a Catalan or move their other knight to c3.

We connect our pawns like usual.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White gets both of their pawns out to control the center.

And we get our knight into the game.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Another option for White is not going for the Catalan and instead opting for more natural development with the Nf3 setup. 

White could go for a bishop move out of the pawn chain before closing it down with e3, followed by development of the light-squared bishop.

These setups don't pose much of a challenge for us because the bishop isn't so active on g5 or f4.

rn1q1rk1/1bpp2pp/1p2pn2/p4p2/2PP4/P3PN2/.text:
And I like this 9...a5 expansion, anticipating that White would like to push their b-pawn. 

Our ideas to finish development are ...Qe7, ...d6 and ...Nbd7. 

We also have that ...Ne4 centralization to go for with a tempo.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/P3PN2/1.text:
We centralize our knight and this is very similar to the Two Knights with Bd2 and Bxc3 lines. 

We'll play ...d6 and ...Nd7 to complete our development.

And let us not forget: ...a5 if b4, and ...g5 are good moves to consider to mount some form of an attack.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP.text:
We can castle as well and we still have access to many of our Dutch ideas. 

White has around 7 moves which I'll cover in the video for this study. 

But basically, you can expect to finish your development and have a dynamic position with nice control of the e4-square.

rn1qk2r/1bpp2pp/1p2pn2/p4p2/1PPP4/P3PN2/.text: After the bishop goes to b2...

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1PPP4/P3PN2/3.text:
Queenside expansion for Bb2 is also a natural idea.

We should nearly always respond to b4 with ...a5. 

The point is that we're challenging White's pawn chain and not letting them have a completely dominant structure on that side of the board.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP1.text:
At this point, both sides will manage to castle. 

However, I like the fact that our development has flowed smoothly.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P3PN2/1P.text:
White brings their bishop out in preparation of castling.

And we can castle.

White may go ahead and prepare castling.

You can go ahead and castle.

rn2k2r/1bppq1pp/1p2pn2/p4p2/1PPP4/P3PN2/.text:
We can continue applying pressure on the b4-pawn. 

The fact that nearly all our pieces are out makes me feel optimistic about this position. 

...Ne4 is coming which would remove the queen's defense from b4. 

If White takes on a5, they'll open up our rook on the a-file.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P3PN2/1.text:
Once a3 comes, it's time to take.

We capture on d2 with check, and White has two recaptures that make sense.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP1.text:
White brings their bishop out to e2.

And we fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P3PN2/1P.text:
The first is just recapturing with the bishop and developing it. 

Bc3 may be a future idea.

We should just develop our bishop.

The idea behind Qxd2 is that the queen can go to c2 in case of ...Ne4 and the bishop could be developed to b2.

We will continue in the same way, developing our bishop. 

Remember, we don't want to go for random knight jumps into e4 when we haven't developed the rest of our pieces.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/4PN2/PP1B.text:
This is the other move that White could play. 

In essence, they argue that if you trade you've moved the same piece twice and helped them develop.

We should just trade because our idea isn't the tempi we spend, but rather our development within the Dutch.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/4PN2/PP1N.text:
Many players, not to give us the trade of bishops, block with the knight.

If we're not pressured, I suggest we shouldn't capture on d2.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP1N1.text:
White recaptures and develops their knight.

And we get ready to fianchetto as we are used to doing.

rnbqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P1N2N2/.text:
This move is played 59% of times, so the transposition is all but probable. 

Besides, there aren't many other better squares for the knight besides c3, specially considering that a3 is often played to give the knight stability on c3.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
Playing 4. e3 early blocks the dark-squared bishop in, and it's chosen 9% of the time.

Our check is perfectly fine, though we could have gone for another setup like the Stonewall. 

We do want to play ...Bb4+ now, as otherwise White can play 5. a3.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P4N2/1P2P.text:
Finally, 4. a3 can be played if your opponent really wants to avoid ...Bb4+.

It's very rare, at only 1%.

But what you'll often find is that this transposes back to the Two Knights chapter.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White plays 3. Nf3 first, which is already a hint that something different from the Two Knights may be played.

And we go for 3...e6, getting ready to give that check on b4 to speed our development up.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays 2. c4, the most popular setup.

We bring our knight out.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
For Study 3, we've already seen that the most common moves White can play for these positions are e3 and a3. 

Sometimes individually, sometimes together. If played early at move 4, White limits the development of their bishop or they lose time.

r1bq1rk1/1pp3pp/p1nppn2/5p2/1PPP4/P4NP1/.text:
Here I recommend 9...a6 with the idea of opening up the a-file if White wants to continue pushing with 10.b5. 

We do have less space, so the engine likes White here. 

After something like 10.0-0, we could try ...Ne7 and ...Bd7 for ...Bc6 to contest the diagonal and begin solving some of our issues.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1n1pp/3p1n2/3Ppp2/2P5/P4NP1/.text:
We can fall back and White has blocked the scope of their g2-bishop.

I like the ...h6 and ...g5 expansion here, with the queen having dynamic possibilities with ...Qe8 to h5 and one of the knights being able to join the party on g6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2np1n2/3Ppp2/2P5/P4NP1/1.text: And if White chooses to push, this is a small inaccuracy.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2np1n2/4pp2/2PP4/P4NP1/1.text:
We can go ahead and push. If White trades on e5, we get a strong central pawn. 

10.dxe5 dxe5 11.Qxd8 Rxd8 isn't good for White because we get a strong rook on the d-file and White doesn't have any active ideas. 

If 10.e3, we can respond with 10...e4! Our position is fine now.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2nppn2/5p2/1PPP4/P4NP1/3.text: White may just go for this expansion before castling.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2nppn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP1.text:
But ...e5 is coming just like in the 7. Nh3 variation. 

...e5 cannot be stopped and if Black achieves this pawn break in the Dutch it's usually a good sign. 

We can go for ...e5 because f5 isn't so weak with the bishop on c8. 

Expect to develop with moves like ...Bd7 and ...Qe7.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2nppn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1P.text:
White usually castles now.

9...e5 is now possible, breaking in the center. 

If there are trades on e5 we would get two strong pawns controlling central squares.
If White plays naturally and castles...

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/3p1n2/4pp2/2PP4/6PN/PP1N.text:
And with this move we've achieved one of the best pawn breaks for Black in the Dutch. 

If 9.dxe5, you can just recapture with 9...dxe5 and you have two strong central pawns. 

If 9.b4, 9...Nc6 is strong. This pawn break allows you great pressure and piece play in the center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PP4/6PN/PP1NP.text:
After White castles kingside, we can already play ...e5. 

Sure, there were some benefits to Nh3, but it does allow an early ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1P1.text:
White develops their knight and blocks the bishop.

And we develop our knight and support e5 some more.

White can now continue with 8.Nf3, controlling the e5-square.

And we should just develop and insist on the possibility of ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P5P1/1P1.text:
White now plays 6.a3 to make us take on d2 and speed their development up.

We have no choice. 

Being the side with less space, trades are convenient.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP1N.text:
The most natural way to develop is to bring out the f-knight.

Because we cannot move our b-pawn, developing our knight to c6 is good, since it also blocks the diagonal.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/6P1/PP1QP.text:
White does have a strong bishop on g2 but they have to develop around it in order not to block it. 

Things on the diagonal are quite complicated, to the point that we may want to go for a slower plan of ...c6, ...d6 and only then something like ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/6PN/PP1NP.text:
Some players who go for early fianchettoes know full well that these squares on the rim like h3 and h6 are good for the knight. 

The knight doesn't block the bishop and it has good options on g5 and f4. A downside is that it doesn't control e5.

7...d6 is our go-to move here, as we clear a square for a queenside piece and we start preparing ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P5P1/1P1B.text:
And now pretty much both recaptures have their merits. 

Here, the queen won't be attacked.

We can continue with our traditional useful pawn move that we play when there's a bishop on g2 already. 

7...d6 to prepare a future ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/P5P1/1P1Q.text:
Capturing with the queen can be played and White will still get two dominant bishops. 

Not much is different here. Let's continue with our ...d6 idea. 

Since there isn't any pressure on our f5-pawn, we can usually play for this in the 3.g3 variations.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/6P1/PP1BP.text:
And blocking with the bishop is White's most common response, played 64% of times.

We should just take.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/6P1/PP1NP.text:
White can just block with the knight as well. If 5.Bd2, the dark squares wouldn't be a problem for Black since the bishops would be traded.

Blocking with the knight therefore makes a little bit more sense, even though it's not as intuitive since development is slowed down.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/6P1/PP1NPP.text:
You'll most likely see this recapture.

But we should just castle. 

As you can see, our main problem is the c8-bishop's development.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/6P1/PP1QPP.text: If the queen recaptures, we can just castle.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
Once White develops their bishop on the long diagonal, we can give our check to develop all our kingside minor pieces.

This is the check we always try to go for.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
The early 3.g3, going for the fianchetto right away, prevents us from playing ...b6, since 4.Bg2 would come with a tempo.

This move happens 3% of the time, but at such an early stage it represents more than 225,000 games at the amateur level.

We should therefore just connect our pawns and forget ideas of ...b6, but still aiming for ...Bb4+.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
After 2.c4 everything seems normal. 

White is controlling central squares with both pawns.

We develop our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 4! 

In this Chapter we'll see third moves that don't involve the knight. 

In Chapter 3, we saw the Catalan with White playing 3.Nf3 first. 3. Nf3 allowed us to still go for ...b6 since the knight blocks the diagonal. 

But if White goes 3. g3, we cannot go ...b6 so easily! Let's see how to fight this!

r1bqk2r/p1pp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPQ2/P.text:
When White develops their knight to e2...

Our bishop jumps into the diagonal and aims at the queen.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPQ2/P.text:
And we should castle as well. We don't have a useful discovery at the moment but that could change. 

I like a plan with connecting rooks by playing ...Qe7, followed by moves like ...d6 and ...g6. 

...g6 is designed to support the f5-pawn and to blunt the d3-bishop a lot more.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/3BPN2/P.text:
We can jump our knight into this central square.

We're going to proceed with 10....d6 and we don't mind any trades on e4. 

After 10.Nxe4 there's a fork with 10...fxe4, and 10.Bxe4 results in 10...fxe4, forcing the knight to a terrible square: e1.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BP2N/P.text:
And here we can castle as well. 

In this variation, although we have less space, we have great control of the e4-square, which is our main idea along with ...d6.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPN2/P.text: And when White gets their queen to e2, trying to play e4...

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1p1/1p2p2p/5p2/2PPn2B/P2BP.text:
We centralize our knight and reveal an attack on the bishop. 

Since we have already played ...h6, I think advancing in the center will be better. 

The engine doesn't approve of ...g5 expansions here, since too many squares are weakened around the king.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BP2N/PP.text: White will most likely castle and defend g2.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPN2/PP.text:
White castles, and so do we. 

If 9.Qc2, aiming for the central push, 9...c5 is a strong idea because it undermines and destabilizes the center, discouraging e4.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P2BPP2/1.text:
Once again, I believe we have explored a setup similar to this one with f3. 

The point is that the bishop's diagonal is blocked and our pieces aren't that good. 

We have less space and we don't have the bishop pair. We can continue by castling.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P2BPP2/1.text:
We can begin preparing our common Dutch ideas. 

Remember that ...g6 has to be played to prepare ...e5 because the bishop on d3 aims at the f5-pawn. 

White still needs engine-like precision to keep their advantage.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/1bPP4/4P3/PP1N.text:
We just recapture with the queen and we're ready to castle. 

A continuation could be 7.a3 and we'll trade on d2 of course, followed by ...b6 and ...Bb7.

rnbq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P3P3/.text:
We should here go for our traditional fianchetto. 

For White to get an advantage, they would need to be aware that variations with f3 are good against this setup. 

Otherwise, after moves like Nf3, expect a fairly easy middlegame with control of the e4-square.

rnbq1rk1/p1ppb1p1/1p2pn1p/5p2/2PP3B/P2BP.text:
White develops, trying to control e4.

And we should control e4 some more.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5p2/1bPP3B/P3P3/1.text:
And after 7. a3, you don't have to take! 

The reason for this is that the knight remains passive on d2.

So I like just coming back to e7. 

I think this is a combination of the knight not being good on d2 and the bishop not being good on h4.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/P3P3/1.text:
It's good to wait for White to force us into a decision.

We should take.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/P3P3/1P.text:
And when the queen recaptures, one of the benefits for us in this position is that we control the light squares a lot more. 

No knight on c3, no queen on c2 to aim at the center, and we've got control of e4.

rnbq1rk1/ppppb1p1/4pn1p/5p2/2PP3B/P3PN2/.text:
Proof of the fact that the knight on d2 isn't ideally placed is that the g1-knight develops to f3, where the d2-knight could have jumped!

This makes the d2-knight rather superfluous.

I like 8...b6 here, getting ready to fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/P2BP3/1.text:
After 6.a3, we have to take on d2.

This is check. 

We cannot leave our bishop on the board because of the lack of space.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BP2N/PP.text:
White could now attempt 7.Nh3. 

From h3, the knight has some useful squares, so it isn't so crazy.

We should fianchetto with a tempo, attacking g2.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPN2/PP.text:
You may see this knight come out to f3, blocking our diagonal.

We should just activate our bishop and control the e4-square.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPQ2/PP.text:
I think we've dealt with Qf3 ideas in the previous chapters. 

Basically, it looks like a tempo for White, but it's actually Black who gets a tempo with the bishop going to b7.

We block the attack and get ready to play 8...Bb7, with a tempo on the queen.

8. d5 allows a fork with 8...Ne5.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P2BP3/1P.text:
Let's say the bishop recaptures.

We can fianchetto and attack g2.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pB1p/5p2/1bPP4/4P3/PP1N.text: If White captures, this is exactly what we wanted.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5p2/1bPP3B/4P3/PP1.text:
White could choose to keep the pin. 

And remember how I've said that once e3 has been played, the bishop cannot be trapped so easily? 

Well, it still holds here, so we should just castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/4P3/PP1.text:
This is one of the unique setups White could go for. 

If 5.Nc3, we transpose into the Nc3 chapter.

Here we should castle and not capture right away. 

The knight isn't going anywhere and our capture on d2 will have the same effect later, so we may as well develop.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/3BP3/PP1B.text:
And we already know that blocking with the bishop is the most popular. 

We don't mind this and we should take.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/3BP3/PP1N.text:
The knight could also block here.

Luckily, we can go for 5...b6 here to fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BP3/PP1N1.text:
Taking with the knight is the most common.

I suggest we play 6...b6 here and get on with fianchettoing our bishop.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BP3/PP1Q1.text:
The queen could also take in this position.

But we can also get ready to fianchetto and be completely fine.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
5.Nc3 transposes to chapter 2.

All we have to do is double the pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1bPP4/4P3/PP1N.text:
5.Nd2 is the unique move.

We should stick to our ...h6 idea.

We want to either force the bishop to trade and activate our queen, or leave the diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/4P3/PP3.text:
White connects their pawns.

Check! If we can play this move with a tempo, we should go ahead.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/3BP3/PP3P.text:
So let's say White plays the third most popular move here besides those transpositions. 

This move is played 9% of the time.

We should just give the check.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/4P3/PP3P.text:
After 4.e3, White argues that they've taken their bishop outside of the pawn chain and have now connected central pawns.

But we still have this check, and because of 4.e3, Bd2 isn't possible.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP1B2/8/PP2PP.text:
Finally, Bf4 is played on move 3 around 1% of the time. This corresponds to more than 76,000 games in the database. 

The idea could simply be to get the bishop out before the pawn chain is connected.

We can go ahead and prepare our check.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/4P3/PP3PP.text:
And suddenly 3.e3 can be played and we seem to be out of book. 

This is played 6% of times and accounts for more than 330,000 amateur games.

We can start preparing our bishop check.

At this point, 4.Nc3 would transpose to chapter 2, and 4.Nf3 transposes to chapter 3!

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5pB1/2PP4/8/PP2PPP.text:
An early 3.Bg5, in the style of the Trompowsky, is also possible. 

This occurred in more than 170,000 games, or in 3% of the games in the database.

I suggest we just defend the knight with the queen and open up our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White goes for 2.c4.

We'll develop our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study! 

After the annoying Catalan, I suppose White could play some bishop move or even a pawn move like 3.e3. 

But we have solutions against these unambitious moves!
